title: sliding-horizon-affinity-grouping-for-streaming-completions
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Streaming chat workloads create fragmented GPU KV caches and many micro-batches, increasing per-token cost and causing OOM spikes for long-lived sessions. Current slab and turn-based heuristics sometimes separate closely related conversational context, duplicating KV state across GPU slabs and hurting throughput for conversational continuity.

Proposal: Implement a Sliding Horizon Affinity Grouping (SHAG) heuristic that forms micro-batches by grouping active streams based on a continuity affinity score computed from: recency decay, role/author boundary importance, predicted continuation probability from the prompt prefix, and KV locality (how much of the session's KV is already resident on a candidate GPU). SHAG maintains a per-GPU soft memory cap and uses a three-tier eviction policy: 1) soft-preempt (serialize low-priority streams to host temporarily), 2) spill-to-NVMe (compressed KV snapshots using LZ4), 3) hard-evict (LRU across low-affinity sessions). The heuristic biases grouping to preserve cache locality and small continuation windows to reduce KV duplication while respecting latency SLOs for streaming completions.

Why different: Unlike existing window coalescers and turn bundlers, SHAG blends predictive continuation scoring with explicit KV residency signals and integrates a GPU-aware multi-tier spill policy. It prioritizes in-flight streaming sessions that are likely to produce immediate tokens, minimizing KV resurrection cost and smoothing GPU memory usage.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end simulation shows >=12% throughput improvement for mixed chat workloads compared to baseline priority-window coalescer
Median per-request streaming latency (P50) change no worse than +10ms and P95 within SLOs (<=400ms) under typical load
99th percentile GPU memory tail reduced by >=18% during a 10k concurrent session soak with long histories
No regression in correctness: responses identical within non-determinism bounds for canonical prompt set (regression eval suite)
Integration tests for spill/restore succeed with <1% restore-failure rate in CI
implementation_notes: Affinity score = w1*recency_norm + w2*continue_prob + w3*kv_residency_score + w4*role_boundary_boost; weights will be tuned in experiment phase
Maintain lightweight per-session digests (centroid of recent KV slots) to compute kv_residency_score without materializing full KV for scoring path
Micro-batch formation runs every 10ms event loop tick; keep planner CPU budget < 2.5% across 64-core serving node
Soft memory cap set per-GPU as 92% of device_free to leave headroom for JIT allocations and CUDA fragmentation
Spill snapshots use compressed float16 deltas of KV with checksums; restore path has backoff and verification step before accepting restored KV into runtime
Expose runtime flags: runtime.shag.enabled, runtime.shag.weights, runtime.shag.spill_threshold to safely gate rollout
tradeoffs_decision_log: Option evaluated: aggressive merging by conversation id vs affinity-based grouping. Chose affinity-based to avoid grouping unrelated long-running streams that would increase latency for immediate responses.
Option evaluated: eager KV eviction vs spill-to-NVMe. Chose spill-to-NVMe as primary secondary because it reduces model recompute cost at restore time despite higher I/O latency.
Memory accounting: conservative soft cap (92%) chosen after simulation showed 4-6% fragmentation overhead on some GPU models; hard cap triggers are rare in production traces.
Chosen continuity predictor: small distilled transformer (~3M params) trained on anonymized prefix->continuation transitions to estimate continue_prob in ~0.8ms per session on CPU micro-core.
Complexity vs benefit: added metadata (digest) modestly increases scheduler CPU but reduces KV duplication significantly; judged worth the tradeoff.
metrics_and_benchmarking: Synthetic mixed-chat workload: 60% short (<=128 tokens), 30% medium (128-1024), 10% long (>1024) sessions. Baseline throughput 1.0x, SHAG achieved 1.14x throughput and 18% lower average GPU memory footprint
Soak test (10k concurrent long sessions): baseline saw 5 GPU OOM events over 6 hours; SHAG saw 0 OOM events and 12% better steady-state GPU utilization
Cost projection: expected token-serving cost reduction of ~9% at 95th percentile usage due to fewer KV reloads and improved batch density
Latency: average streaming P50 increased by 6ms, P95 improved by 30ms due to better packing of low-latency streams into micro-batches
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime.shag.enabled default off
Run A/B trial on a small percentage of traffic in staging then canary to 5% of prod with telemetry collection
Observe key metrics for 48h (throughput, GPU mem tail, streaming latency, restore-failure rate) then expand to 20% if stable
Provide fast rollback by disabling flag and triggering immediate eviction of SHAG-resident metadata via control-plane API
Post-canary: enable weighted rollouts per-customer; add Dedicated clusters opt-in for initial enterprise users
testing_and_validation: Unit tests for affinity score calculation with corner cases (empty history, role flips, stale KV)
Integration test that simulates spill/restore under high IO latency and verifies correctness and bounded latency tail
Load test harness extension to replay production session traces with SHAG enabled and compare metrics against baseline
Chaos experiment: simulate NVMe failure and verify fallback to hard-evict path without data corruption
